candidate.answerReason: Taking reciprocals produces three linear relations in 1/x, 1/y, and 1/z. Adding the first two and subtracting the third isolates 2/x. For any original solution, the final denominator is necessarily nonzero.

methods.label: Take reciprocals to obtain linear relations
methods.explanation:
The numerators are products and the denominators are sums, so taking reciprocals will separate the variables. The original fractions must be defined. Since \(a,b,c\ne0\), their numerators are nonzero, which implies \(x,y,z\ne0\). Thus all the following reciprocals are valid:
\[
\frac1a=\frac1x+\frac1y,
\qquad
\frac1b=\frac1x+\frac1z,
\]
\[
\frac1c=\frac1y+\frac1z.
\]
These equations are linear in \(1/x,1/y,1/z\). Adding the first two and subtracting the third cancels the unwanted terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac2x
&=\frac1a+\frac1b-\frac1c\\
&=\frac{bc+ac-ab}{abc}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(abc\ne0\) and \(2/x\ne0\), the numerator \(ac+bc-ab\) is also nonzero. Multiplying by the nonzero denominators and solving gives
\[
x=\frac{2abc}{ac+bc-ab},
\]
which is choice E. This conclusion applies whenever the original defined equations have a solution.
methods.levelReason: Reciprocals turn the problem into elementary addition and subtraction of three linear equations.

methods.label: Express y and z in terms of x
methods.explanation:
We can eliminate \(y\) and \(z\) by solving the first two equations for them. Assume throughout that the original fractions are defined. Their nonzero values \(a,b,c\) imply \(x,y,z\ne0\).

Clearing the first denominator gives
\[
xy=a(x+y),\qquad y(x-a)=ax.
\]
Here \(x\ne a\): otherwise this equation would give \(0=a^2\), contrary to \(a\ne0\). Similarly, \(x\ne b\). Therefore
\[
y=\frac{ax}{x-a},\qquad z=\frac{bx}{x-b}.
\]
Adding these expressions gives
\[
y+z=\frac{x((a+b)x-2ab)}{(x-a)(x-b)}.
\]
Since \(y+z\ne0\), the factor \((a+b)x-2ab\) is nonzero. We may now substitute into the third equation and cancel the nonzero common factors:
\[
c=\frac{yz}{y+z}=\frac{abx}{(a+b)x-2ab}.
\]
Clearing this denominator and collecting the terms containing \(x\) yields
\[
(ac+bc-ab)x=2abc.
\]
The right side is nonzero, so \(ac+bc-ab\ne0\). Hence
\[
x=\frac{2abc}{ac+bc-ab},
\]
choice E, for every solution of the original defined equations.
methods.levelReason: This alternative uses ordinary equation rearrangement and rational-expression operations, with each division justified.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task asks for a consequence of rational equations while preserving their domain, matching the rational-equation solving component of cnm_165. Reciprocal concepts and three-variable linear elimination belong only to the first route. Mixed rational operations and collecting linear terms belong to the substitution route. Denominator definedness and rational-expression addition support both.
limitations: The formula applies to parameter triples admitting a solution of the original defined equations. Nonzero a, b, and c alone do not guarantee that such a solution exists.

review.mathematicalCheck: Reciprocal elimination gives \(2/x=(ac+bc-ab)/(abc)\). Direct substitution independently gives \((ac+bc-ab)x=2abc\). Both routes justify every introduced division and establish that the final denominator is nonzero for an original solution.
